The Coverage Principle:
How Pre-training Enables Post-Training

Abstract

Language models demonstrate remarkable abilities when pre-trained on large text corpora and fine-tuned for specific tasks, but how and why pre-training shapes the success of the final model remains poorly understood. Notably, although pre-training success is often quantified by cross entropy loss, cross-entropy can be a poor predictor of downstream performance. Instead, we provide a theoretical perspective on this relationship through the lens of coverage, which quantifies the probability mass the pre-trained model places on high-quality responses and which is necessary and sufficient for post-training and test-time scaling methods such as Best-of-N to succeed. Our main results develop an understanding of the coverage principle, a phenomenon whereby next-token prediction implicitly optimizes toward a model with good coverage. In particular, we uncover a mechanism that explains the power of coverage in predicting downstream performance: coverage generalizes faster than cross entropy, avoiding spurious dependence on problem-dependent parameters such as the sequence length. We also study practical algorithmic interventions with provable benefits for improving coverage, including (i) model/checkpoint selection procedures, (ii) gradient normalization schemes, and (iii) test-time decoding strategies.

1 Introduction

The remarkable capabilities of language models stem from a two-stage training process: (1) large-scale pre-training via next-token prediction with the cross-entropy loss (predicting what token should follow a prefix) and (2) targeted post-training—typically via reinforcement learning—to adapt the model to specific domains and tasks. Investing more compute and data into pre-training often enables post-training to produce a stronger model, but theoretical understanding of how these stages interact is limited. Indeed, despite substantial investment into scaling pre-training (Gadre et al., 2025; Sardana et al., 2024; Hoffmann et al., 2022), several works have demonstrated that starting post-training from a better next-token predictor does not ensure stronger performance on downstream tasks (Liu et al., 2022; Zeng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Lourie et al., 2025; Springer et al., 2025). Motivated by this disconnect, we theoretically investigate the connection between pre-training objectives and downstream success, asking:

Can we precisely characterize the relationship between the next-token prediction loss and downstream performance? What metrics are most predictive of downstream success?

Motivated by the recent interest in test-time scaling, we focus our attention on post-training via Best-of-NN (BoN) sampling or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. For a prompt xx, Best-of-N draws nn responses yy from the model and returns the best response according to a task-specific reward. Several prior works have demonstrated that the performance of BoN is strongly indicative of how well the model will perform after post-training via reinforcement learning (Yue et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).

Our starting point is the observation that cross-entropy alone cannot provide meaningful answers to the questions above; see Fig. 1, which illustrates that cross-entropy can be anti-correlated with BoN performance, echoing Chen et al. (2025). Instead, we show that the missing link is the coverage profile , a refinement of cross-entropy that explicitly quantifies the model’s ability to assign sufficient probability to rare but high-quality responses.

{definition}

[Coverage profile] The coverage profile of a model π^\widehat{\pi} for a distribution π\pi is

CovN(π∥π^):=ℙx∼μ,y∼π(⋅∣x)[π⁡(y∣x)π^​(y∣x)≥N],\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})\vcentcolon=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{\mu},y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid{}x)}\left[\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\widehat{\pi}(y\mid{}x)}\geq{}N\right], (1)

where N≥1N\geq 1 is the number of Best-of-N sampling attempts. Here, yy is the full response when prompted with xx, π\pi represents the pre-training data distribution, which we presuppose covers downstream tasks of interest, and π^\widehat{\pi} is the pre-trained model. We prove that a good coverage profile is necessary and sufficient for Best-of-N to succeed (see Section 2, as well as Sections D.2 and D.2). This is highlighted in Fig. 1, where we find that the coverage profile is correlated with downstream performance for Best-of-N (which is exactly 𝖯𝖺𝗌𝗌​@​N\mathsf{Pass@}{N}), even when cross-entropy is not.11 1 Formally, the coverage profile refines cross-entropy/KL divergence; see Section 2.1. Motivated by this characterization of BoN performance, we ask: When, and through what mechanism, does next-token prediction produce a model π^\widehat{\pi} with good coverage?

1.1 Contributions

We develop a theoretical understanding of the coverage principle, whereby next-token prediction implicitly optimizes toward a model with good coverage, inheriting the training corpus’ coverage over tasks of interest.

Cross-entropy: Scaling laws and limitations (Section 3)

We begin by deriving provable scaling laws that link cross-entropy—specifically, a certain sequence-level notion—to coverage and hence downstream performance, but show that cross-entropy can be sensitive to sequence length and other problem parameters, leading to vacuous predictions; this motivates our main results.

Next-token prediction implicitly optimizes coverage (Section 4)

The first of our main theoretical results (Section 4) is a new generalization analysis for next-token prediction (more generally, maximum likelihood) that exploits the unique structure of the logarithmic loss to show that coverage can generalize faster than cross entropy; we refer to this as the coverage principle. Concretely, our analysis shows that the coverage profile for models learned with next-token prediction (i) avoids spurious dependence on problem-dependent parameters such as sequence length (in contrast to cross-entropy), and (ii) converges faster still as the tail parameter NN is increased. Our analysis—which is similar in spirit to Mendelson’s small ball method (Mendelson, 2014; Mendelson, 2017)—can be viewed as a giving a new, fine-grained understanding of maximum likelihood (Wong and Shen, 1995; van de Geer, 2000; Zhang, 2006), which we expect to be of broader interest.

Stochastic gradient descent through the lens of coverage (Section 5)

The preceding results apply to general model classes Π\Pi, but consider the empirical maximizer of the next-token prediction (maximum likelihood) objective, in the vein of classical techniques in learning theory. For the second of our main results, we focus on a specific model class—overparameterized autoregressive linear models (3)—but take a more realistic approach and analyze stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the next-token prediction objective, in the one-pass (“compute-optimal”) regime. We show that while SGD provably optimizes the coverage profile, it experiences suboptimal dependence on the sequence length HH. We then show that gradient normalization (which is loosely connected to Adam-like updates (Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024)) provably improves coverage, removing dependence on the sequence length. We also consider the expert distillation setting where πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} represents a teacher network for which token-level logits are available, and give a novel gradient normalization scheme which enjoys improves coverage even further.

Interventions for better coverage (Section 6)

Finally, we look beyond standard next-token prediction and explore families of new interventions aimed at improving coverage in theory.
(i) Test-time (Section 6.1). We show that for standard token-level SGD, a new test-time decoding strategy inspired by test-time training (Sun et al., 2020; Akyürek et al., 2025) provably improves coverage.
(ii) Model/checkpoint selection (Section 6.3). For selecting the best model (or checkpoint) from a small number of candidates, we give tournament procedures that enjoy significantly better coverage profile (particularly with respect to the tail parameter NN) than naïve validation with cross-entropy.

Additional results (Appendix E)

Beyond the results above, we show that coverage profile satisfies additional properties, including: (1) maximum likelihood can find models with low coverage even in the presence of severe misspecification (e.g., even if no model with low cross entropy exists) (Section E.1); (2) coverage can generalize better under additional structural properties of the model class such as convexity (Section E.1).

In summary, we believe that coverage offers a new perspective on the connection between pre-training objectives and downstream post-training success. Our results demonstrate that this perspective is mathematically rich and fundamental, opening the door to a deeper understanding. To this end, we highlight a number of fascinating directions for future research in Section 7.

2 Problem Setup

We now introduce the formal problem setup for the remainder of the paper.

Next-token prediction and maximum likelihood

We work in the following setting, which subsumes next-token prediction: 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the prompt space, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is the response space, and πD:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi_{\texttt{D}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) is the data distribution. We are given a dataset 𝒟={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}},y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}})\right\}_{i=1}^{n} where xi∼μx^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\sim\mathcal{\mu} and yi∼πD(⋅∣xi)y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\sim\pi_{\texttt{D}}(\cdot\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}). We consider the maximum likelihood objective

L^n​(π):=∑i=1nlog⁡π⁡(yi∣xi).\displaystyle\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi)\vcentcolon=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\pi(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}). (2)

and refer to π^:=arg​maxπ∈Π⁡L^n​(π)\widehat{\pi}\vcentcolon={}\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi}\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi) as the maximum likelihood estimator for a user-specified model class Π\Pi. This is a generalization of the next-token prediction, where 𝒴=𝒱H\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{V}^{H} is a token sequence and π(y∣x)=∏h=1Hπ(yh∣x,y1:h−1)\pi(y\mid{}x)=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\pi(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1}) is explicitly autoregressive, so that L^n(π)=∑i=1n∑h=1Hlogπ(yhi∣xi,y1:h−1i)\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\log\pi(y_{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}},y_{1:h-1}^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}). We specialize to next-token prediction at certain points but otherwise focus on the general setting. We make the following realizability assumption throughout. {assumption}[Realizability] The data distribution πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} is realizable by some model π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. This formulation captures pre-training and supervised fine-tuning, with some caveats; see Section 7.1.

Post-training and the coverage profile

Given a reward function rT​(x,y)∈{0,1}r_{\texttt{T}}(x,y)\in\left\{0,1\right\} representing success at a downstream task T, the goal is to fine-tune π^\widehat{\pi}—through reinforcement learning or test-time scaling—to obtain near-optimal reward. We show (Sections D.2 and D.2) that for any task-specific comparator policy πT:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi_{\texttt{T}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}), Best-of-N sampling with Θ~​(N)\widetilde{\Theta}(N) samples satisfies 𝔼x∼μ[rT(x,πT(x))−rT(x,π^BoN(x))]≍CovN(πT∥π^)\En_{x\sim\mathcal{\mu}}\left[r_{\texttt{T}}(x,\pi_{\texttt{T}}(x))-r_{\texttt{T}}(x,\widehat{\pi}^{\texttt{BoN}}(x))\right]\asymp\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\texttt{T}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi}), so a good coverage profile for πT\pi_{\texttt{T}} is sufficient for high reward. Further, while less well understood, some form of coverage is thought to be necessary for the success of post-training methods like GRPO (Yue et al., 2025).

Returning to pre-training, it is clear that there is little hope that next-token prediction will produce a model π^\widehat{\pi} with good coverage with respect to a downstream task unless the data distribution πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} itself has reasonable coverage with respect to this task. We therefore posit that the data distribution covers such a downstream task, in the sense that it includes high-reward responses with some bounded-below probability. Since coverage satisfies a transitivity property, it follows that coverage with respect to πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} implies coverage with respect to the optimal policy for the downstream task. For example, if πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} has a 10% chance of generating a correct response, and CovN/10(πD∥π^)=ε\texttt{Cov}_{N/10}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})=\varepsilon, then we get 10​ε10\varepsilon error.22 2 See Section D.1 for formal results. Thus, going forward, we focus on understanding when next-token prediction achieves good coverage CovN(πD∥π^)\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;{}\widehat{\pi}) relative to the data distribution πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} itself, and avoid concerning ourselves with specific details of the task policy πT\pi_{\texttt{T}} or the specific relationship between πT\pi_{\texttt{T}} and πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}.

Autoregressive linear models

We analyze next-token prediction and maximum likelihood for general model classes Π\Pi, but our running example throughout the paper will be the class Π\Pi of autoregressive linear models, defined by a known feature map ϕ:𝒳×𝒱⋆→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{V}^{\star}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}. For each parameter θ∈Θ⊂ℝd\theta\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, the model πθ=(πθ)h=1H\pi_{\theta}=(\pi_{\theta})_{h=1}^{H} is defined by

πθ(yh∣x,y1:h−1)∝exp(⟨θ,ϕ(x,y1:h)⟩).\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:linear}\pi_{\theta}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})\propto\exp(\langle\theta,\phi(x,y_{1:h})\rangle). (3)

In practice, autoregressive sequence models—such as those based on transformers—generate each token by sampling from a softmax distribution whose logits are given by a linear combination of learned features (Radford et al., 2019). Eq. 3 simplifies this by freezing the feature map, yet remains expressive enough to model complex non-Markovian dependencies, depending on the choice of features.

{assumption}

We assume Θ⊆{θ:‖θ‖≤1}\Theta\subseteq\left\{\theta:\|\theta\|\leq 1\right\} is convex, and suph,x,y1:h∥ϕ(x,y1:h)∥≤B\sup_{h,x,y_{1:h}}\|\phi(x,y_{1:h})\|\leq B for some B≥1B\geq{}1.

2.1 Properties of the Coverage Profile

Before proceeding, we briefly discuss some properties of the coverage profile that will be helpful to keep in mind.

{remark}

[Coverage profile as a refinement of cross-entropy] The coverage profile can be viewed as a fine-grained, inference budget-sensitive refinement of cross-entropy. Concretely, if we write

CovN(πD∥π^)=ℙπD[logπD​(y∣x)π^​(y∣x)≥logN],\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})=\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y\mid{}x)}{\widehat{\pi}(y\mid{}x)}\geq{}\log{}N\right], (4)

it becomes clear that the coverage profile is simply the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the log density ratio X:=log⁡πD​(y∣x)π^​(y∣x)X\vcentcolon=\log\frac{\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y\mid{}x)}{\widehat{\pi}(y\mid{}x)}, while KL-divergence corresponds to the mean: 𝔼πD⁡[X]\En_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}\left[X\right]. It is well known that the CDF of a random variable is a more informative statistic than its mean (Durrett, 2019); the former can be much more sensitive to the model’s behavior at the tail than the latter. Indeed, the coverage profile can behave very differently across scales, as shown by Fig. 1.33 3 Interestingly, we show (Section D.1) that if the coverage profile satisfies a certain growth condition uniformly for all scales MM, then it implies a bound on KL-divergence—a weak converse to Section 3.

{remark}

[KL divergence and coverage profile are not estimable] We emphasize that KL-divergence and the coverage profile are not estimable quantities in general, due to the fact both depend on the unknown density πD​(y∣x)\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y\mid{}x) for the data distribution. This motivates the use of cross-entropy in practice, as the former is an estimable upper bound on D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^)D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right). Analogously, we show in Section 6.3 that various estimable proxies for the coverage profile can be used to select models with good coverage. One exception is the expert distillation setting (see Section 6.2), where πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} is a teacher network for which the log-probabilities log⁡πD​(y∣x)\log\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y\mid{}x) are available.

3 Cross-Entropy and Coverage: Scaling Laws and Limitations

A natural approach to understanding when next-token prediction achieves good coverage is to appeal to cross-entropy—perhaps first showing that next-token prediction achieves low cross-entropy (which is true asymptotically), and then relating cross-entropy to coverage. In this section we motivate our main results by showing that while this is possible in a weak sense, it does not yield predictive guarantees for downstream performance in the finite-sample regime.

Define the sequence-level cross-entropy for π^\widehat{\pi} as D𝖢𝖤(πD∥π^):=𝔼πD[∑h=1Hlog1π^(yh∣x,y1:h−1)]D_{\mathsf{CE}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\vcentcolon=\En_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{H}\log\frac{1}{\widehat{\pi}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})}\right]. Since 𝔼𝒟​∼i.i.d.​πD[L^n(π)]=−n⋅D𝖢𝖤(πD∥π)\En_{\mathcal{D}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\pi_{\texttt{D}}}\big[\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi)\big]=-n\cdot D_{\mathsf{CE}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi\right), one expects that as we scale up compute, number of samples nn, and model capacity Π\Pi, D𝖢𝖤(πD∥π^)→D𝖢𝖤(πD∥πD)D_{\mathsf{CE}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\to D_{\mathsf{CE}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{D}}\right), or equivalently D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^)→0D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\to{}0, where D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^):=𝔼πD[∑h=1HlogπD(yh∣x,y1:h−1)π^(yh∣x,y1:h−1)]D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\vcentcolon=\En_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{H}\log\frac{\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})}{\widehat{\pi}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})}\right] is the sequence-level KL divergence.

A simple scaling law for cross-entropy

We show below that if the model π^\widehat{\pi} has reasonable KL divergence to the data distribution, the coverage profile can be bounded:{proposition}[KL-to-coverage; see Section D.1] For all N≥eN\geq{}e, CovN(πD∥π^)≤D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^)log⁡(N/e)\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})\leq\frac{D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)}{\log(N/e)}. Combining Section 3 with Section D.2 and our assumption that πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} has good coverage with respect to the downstream task yields a simple “scaling law” for test-time compute with BoN:

That is, for a fixed model π^\widehat{\pi} and KL-divergence level D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^)≤D𝖢𝖤(πD∥π^)D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\leq D_{\mathsf{CE}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right), Eq. 5 predicts that test-time compute should increase exponentially with the desired accuracy ε\varepsilon.44 4 Neither KL divergence nor the coverage profile are observable quantities (though cross entropy is an estimable upper bound on KL), so this is a theoretical prediction rather than a practical one as-is; see Section 2.1.

Insufficiency of cross-entropy

At first glance, this seems to be in line with empirical test-time scaling laws (OpenAI, 2024), but there is an issue: While token-level cross-entropy has been observed to be modest in contemporary language models (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2022), the sequence-level cross-entropy (and KL-divergence) generally grows with the length HH of the sequence, so that Eq. 5 predicts exponential test-time scaling in the sequence length. Moreover, such a law cannot hold if we only assume token-level cross-entropy is bounded; see Section D.2.

Is this the end of the story? On the one hand, it is simple to show (Section D.1) that Section 3 is tight for a worst-case pair of models. Moreover, even for the autoregressive linear model in Eq. 3, sequence-level KL divergence scales linearly with the sequence length HH, as shown in the next result. {proposition} Fix H∈ℕH\in\mathbb{N} and d=1d=1. There exists a feature map ϕ:𝒳×𝒱⋆→[−1,1]\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{V}^{\star}\to[-1,1] and induced autoregressive linear class Π\Pi with parameter space Θ=[−1,1]\Theta=[-1,1], distribution μ\mu over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, such that for any proper estimator π^=π^​(𝒟)∈Π\widehat{\pi}=\widehat{\pi}(\mathcal{D})\in\Pi, there exists data distribution πD∈Π\pi_{\texttt{D}}\in\Pi such that with probability at least 0.250.25,

D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^)≥H4​n.\displaystyle D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\geq\frac{H}{4n}. (6)

This behavior is reflected empirically in Fig. 2 for a graph reasoning task. Yet, for this task, we find (Fig. 2) that in spite of large cross-entropy/KL, next-token prediction learns a model π^\widehat{\pi} with a good coverage profile across a range of sequence lengths and that downstream Best-of-N succeeds. Why is this happening? In light of the discussion above, it must be related to specific inductive bias of the next-token prediction objective itself.

A glimmer of hope: Case study in Bernoulli models

To see why large cross-entropy may not be a barrier to coverage, consider perhaps the simplest setting, Bernoulli models, where 𝒳={⟂}\mathcal{X}=\{\perp\}, 𝒴={0,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\}, Π={Ber⁡(p)}p∈(0,1/2)\Pi=\left\{\mathrm{Ber}(p)\right\}_{p\in(0,1/2)}, and πD=Ber⁡(p⋆)\pi_{\texttt{D}}=\mathrm{Ber}(p^{\star}) for some small p⋆∈(0,1/2)p^{\star}\in(0,1/2).

The maximum likelihood model is π^=Ber⁡(p^)\widehat{\pi}=\mathrm{Ber}(\widehat{p}), where p^\widehat{p} is the empirical frequency of y=1y=1 in the dataset. We observe that with positive probability (and constant probability if n≤1/p⋆n\leq\nicefrac{{1}}{{p^{\star}}}), the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} will only contain examples where y=0y=0, so that the maximum likelihood model is π^=Ber⁡(0)\widehat{\pi}=\mathrm{Ber}(0). This implies that expected KL divergence is infinite: 𝔼[D𝖪𝖫(πD∥π^)]=+∞\En\left[D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\widehat{\pi}\right)\right]=+\infty. However, the coverage profile turns out to be well-behaved; to see this, we consider two cases:

  1. 1.

    If n≳log⁡(δ−1)/p⋆n\gtrsim\nicefrac{{\log(\delta^{-1})}}{{p^{\star}}}, a Binomial tail bound implies that p^≥p⋆2\widehat{p}\geq\frac{p^{\star}}{2} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, so Cov2(πD∥π^)=0\texttt{Cov}_{2}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})=0.

  2. 2.

    If n≲log⁡(δ−1)/p⋆n\lesssim\nicefrac{{\log(\delta^{-1})}}{{p^{\star}}}, we can bound CovN(πD∥π^)≤p⋆≲log⁡(δ−1)n\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})\leq{}p^{\star}\lesssim\frac{\log(\delta^{-1})}{n} by simply writing off the missing mass.

Combining these cases, we see that CovN(πD∥π^)≲log⁡(δ−1)n\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\;\|\;\widehat{\pi})\lesssim{}\frac{\log(\delta^{-1})}{n} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta for all N≥2N\geq{}2; this gives hope that even though cross-entropy itself is infinite, maximum likelihood may actually learn a model with good coverage in the background. In what follows, we will show that this is not a fluke, but a general phenomenon.

{remark}

[Missing mass] The underlying issue in both of the preceding examples is missing mass: there are responses that even a well-generalizing learner will fail to cover, and for these we may incur a large contribution to the KL-divergence. More generally, KL-divergence and cross-entropy are susceptible to contributions of the scale log⁡Wmax\log W_{\texttt{max}} where Wmax=maxπ∈Π⁡‖πDπ‖∞W_{\texttt{max}}=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\left\|\frac{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}{\pi}\right\|_{\infty} (which could be as large as HH, as in Section 3) when the model does not have enough information to generalize/extrapolate. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced when the prompt distribution is heterogeneous.

4 Next-Token Prediction Implicitly Optimizes Coverage

We now present our main result (Section 4): due to the unique structure of the logarithmic loss, maximum likelihood can learn models with a good coverage profile even when the cross-entropy is vacuously large. Henceforth, we abbreviate CovN(π):=CovN(πD∥π)\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi)\vcentcolon=\texttt{Cov}_{N}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi\right). We make use of the following covering number.

{definition}

For a class Π\Pi and α≥0\alpha\geq 0, we let 𝒩∞​(Π,α)\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha) denote the size of the smallest cover Π′⊂{𝒳→Δ(𝒴)}\Pi^{\prime}\subset\left\{\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})\right\} such that for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, there exists π′∈Π′\pi^{\prime}\in\Pi^{\prime} such that supx∈𝒳,y∈𝒴|log⁡π⁡(y∣x)−log⁡π′​(y∣x)|≤α\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X},y\in\mathcal{Y}}\lvert\log\pi(y\mid x)-\log\pi^{\prime}(y\mid x)\rvert\leq\alpha. {theorem}[Fast generalization for coverage] Fix N≥8N\geq 8 and let c>0c>0 be an absolute constant. Suppose Section 2 holds. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the maximum likelihood estimator π^:=arg​maxπ∈Π⁡L^n​(π)\widehat{\pi}\vcentcolon=\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi}\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi) has

CovN(π^)≲1log⁡N⋅infε>0{log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,ε)n+ε}⏟=:𝒞fine(Π,n)+log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,c​log⁡N)+log⁡(δ−1)n⏟=:𝒞coarse(Π,N,n).\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\lesssim\frac{1}{\log{}N}\cdot\underbrace{\inf_{\varepsilon>0}\left\{\frac{\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\varepsilon)}{n}+\varepsilon\right\}}_{=\vcentcolon\;\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{fine}}(\Pi,n)}+\underbrace{\frac{\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}\left(\Pi,c\log{}N\right)+\log(\delta^{-1})}{n}}_{=\vcentcolon\;\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{coarse}}(\Pi,N,n)}. (7)

Eq. 7 has a fine-grained term 𝒞fine​(Π,n)\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{fine}}(\Pi,n) and coarse-grained term 𝒞coarse​(Π,N,n)\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{coarse}}(\Pi,N,n); we interpret each below.

Fine-grained term. 𝒞fine​(Π,n)\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{fine}}(\Pi,n) evaluates the covering number 𝒩∞​(Π,ε)\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\varepsilon) at a small scale ε\varepsilon (typically ε≈poly⁡(1/n)\varepsilon\approx\mathrm{poly}(1/n)), which matches typical bounds for conditional density estimation (e.g., Bilodeau et al. (2023)) in KL divergence; however, unlike KL-based bounds this term has no explicit dependence on sequence length HH or density ratios log⁡Wmax\log W_{\texttt{max}}. The term is further scaled by 1/log⁡N1/\log{}N, which implies that coverage enjoys faster convergence as we move further into the tail by increasing NN; this reflects the unique structure of the logarithmic loss, and may be viewed as a new form of implicit bias.

Summarizing, the fine-grained term in Eq. 7 witnesses the phenomenon we term the coverage principle: the coverage profile enjoys faster generalization than cross-entropy; roughly, the rate is what we would expect (via Section 3) if we could somehow control KL without paying for the sequence length HH or density ratio log⁡Wmax\log W_{\texttt{max}}. See Appendix B for a detailed comparison to standard (asymptotic and non-asymptotic) generalization bounds for maximum likelihood based on Hellinger distance and KL-divergence.

Coarse-grained term. The coarse-grained term 𝒞coarse​(Π,N,n)\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{coarse}}(\Pi,N,n) captures the missing mass phenomenon exemplified by the Bernoulli example in the prequel. This term is not explicitly normalized by 1/log⁡N1/\log{}N (compared to the fine-grained term), but depends on the covering number 𝒩∞​(Π,α)\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha) only at a very large scale α≈log⁡N\alpha\approx\log{}N. As such, the dependence on the complexity/richness of Π\Pi in this term vanishes as we increase NN.

Overall, while the guarantee in Eq. 7 might look surprising at first glance (particularly the coarse term, as we are not aware of any existing generalization bounds with dependence on covering numbers at such a large scale), we show in Section 4.3 (Appendix H) that both terms are tight in general.

Coverage can converge under severe misspecification

In Section 4, we assume realizability, i.e., the data distribution πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} lies within the model class Π\Pi (Section 2). In the general misspecified setting where πD∉Π\pi_{\texttt{D}}\notin\Pi, the coverage may instead scale with the approximation error minπ∈ΠD𝖪𝖫(πD∥π)\min_{\pi\in\Pi}D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi\right) (Section E.2), which is undesirable. Nevertheless, we show that when Π\Pi is convex, the MLE in fact enjoys a better coverage bound that depends only on the coverage profile of the best-in-class approximate of πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} (Section E.1). Further, in Section 6.3, we propose tournament-style estimators with coverage guarantees scaling with minπ∈Π⁡CovN​(π)\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi) for any (possibly misspecified, non convex) class Π\Pi.

4.1 Examples

To build intuition, we analyze the behavior of Section 4 under a general growth assumption on the covering number, then specialize to autoregressive linear models, showing how they exemplify the coverage principle.

{corollary}

(i) Parametric regime: Suppose that there are parameters d≥2d\geq 2 and C≥2C\geq 2 such that log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,α)≤d​log⁡(C/α)\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha)\leq d\log(C/\alpha) for α∈(0,C/2]\alpha\in(0,C/2]. Then for any N≥8N\geq 8, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

CovN​(π^)≲d⁡[[log⁡(C/log⁡N)]++log⁡(C​n)log⁡N]+log⁡(1/δ)n.\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\lesssim\frac{d\left[\left[\log(C/\log N)\right]_{+}+\frac{\log(Cn)}{\log N}\right]+\log(1/\delta)}{n}.

(ii) Nonparametric regime: Suppose that there are parameters C≥2C\geq 2 and p>0p>0 such that log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,α)≤(C/α)p\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha)\leq(C/\alpha)^{p} for α∈(0,C/2]\alpha\in(0,C/2]. Then for any N≥8N\geq 8 and n≥log1/p⁡N⋅(C/log⁡N)pn\geq{}\log^{1/p}N\cdot(C/\log{}N)^{p}, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

CovN​(π^)≲1log⁡N​(Cpn)1p+1+log⁡(1/δ)n.\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\lesssim\frac{1}{\log N}\left(\frac{C^{p}}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{p+1}}+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}.

This result shows that for sufficiently rich classes (e.g., when p>0p>0), the fine-grained term dominates the coarse-grained term for nn sufficently large. On the other hand, for simple classes (e.g., when p=0p=0), the coarse-grained term can dominate the fine-grained term.

Autoregressive linear models: Low dimension

We now consider the autoregressive linear model in Eq. 3. When the dimension dd is small, this class satisfies log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,α)≍d​log⁡(B​H/α)\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha)\asymp{}d\log(BH/\alpha) (corresponding to the parametric regime in Section 4.1), which gives the following coverage upper bound for next-token prediction. {corollary} Consider the autoregressive linear model in Eq. 3. For any N≥8N\geq 8, it holds that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, next-token prediction achieves

CovN​(π^)≲d⁡[[log⁡(B​H/log⁡N)]++log⁡(B​H​n)log⁡N]+log⁡(1/δ)n.\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\lesssim\frac{d\left[\left[\log(BH/\log N)\right]_{+}+\frac{\log(BHn)}{\log N}\right]+\log(1/\delta)}{n}.

Thus—in line with the coverage principle—coverage generalizes in a (nearly) horizon-independent fashion for autoregressive linear models, in stark contrast to the cross-entropy lower bound in Section 3. The only drawback (which is fundamental) is that since the class has low capacity, the coarse-grained term dominates for most parameter regimes, and the improvement as NN scales is quite modest.

Autoregressive linear models: High dimension

As a more interesting example, we next look at the behavior of next-token prediction for autoregressive linear models in an “overparameterized” regime where the dimension dd is arbitrarily large (Zhang, 2002; Neyshabur et al., 2015; Bartlett et al., 2017). Here, we control the richness of the class Π\Pi by the norm parameter BB. In this regime, it turns out that in the worst-case, the capacity log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,α)\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha) scales polynomially in HH. To address, this we prove a refined version of Section 4 that adapts to the variance in the data distribution πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}, avoiding explicit dependence on sequence length.

Define the inherent variance for the data distribution as

σ⋆2:=𝔼πD[∑h=1H∥ϕ(x,y1:h)−\macc@depthΔ\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a111(x,y1:h−1)πD∥2],\displaystyle\sigma_{\star}^{2}\vcentcolon=\En_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{H}\big\|\phi(x,y_{1:h})-\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}(x,y_{1:h-1})\big\|^{2}\right], (8)

where \macc@depthΔ\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a111(x,y1:h−1)πD:=𝔼yh∼πD(⋅∣x,y1:h−1)[ϕ(x,y1:h)]\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{}_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}(x,y_{1:h-1})\vcentcolon=\En_{y_{h}\sim\pi_{\texttt{D}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{1:h-1})}\left[\phi(x,y_{1:h})\right] is the average feature vector given the prefix (x,y1:h−1)(x,y_{1:h-1}). We can interpret the inherent variance σ⋆2\sigma_{\star}^{2} as a notion of effective sequence length; it captures the number tokens that are “pivotal” in the sense that they have high variation conditioned on the prefix; the name reflects a noted phenomenon in language modeling that most tokens are near-deterministic and easy to predict given their prefix, with only a few having high entropy (Abdin et al., 2024). For any N≥2N\geq 2, next-token prediction achieves

𝔼⁡[CovN​(π^)]≲σ⋆2n⋅log⁡N+B2n.\displaystyle\En\left[\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\right]\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{n\cdot\log N}}+\frac{B^{2}}{n}. (9)

Similar to Section 4, the first term in Eq. 9 can be viewed as “fine-grained” and the second term as “coarse-grained”; the former is typically larger, but decreases with the tail parameter NN, while the latter does not decrease with NN but is typically smaller to begin with. We prove (details in Section I.8) that this result is tight in the sense that if σ⋆2≍H\sigma_{\star}^{2}\asymp{}H, n≥Hn\geq{}H is indeed necessary to achieve good non-trivial coverage in the overparameterized regime.

We mention in passing that we view the introduction of the inherent variance σ⋆2\sigma_{\star}^{2} as an instance-dependent notion of complexity for autoregressive models to be a non-trivial conceptual contribution, which may find broader use.

4.2 Proof Sketch

The basic idea behind the proof of Section 4 is to interpret the condition CovN​(π)≥ε\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi)\geq{}\varepsilon as an small-ball like anti-concentration condition in the vein of Mendelson (2014); Mendelson (2017). That is, for models π∈Π\pi\in\Pi where coverage is large, the condition CovN​(π)≥ε\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi)\geq{}\varepsilon witnesses a one-sided tail bound which implies that the empirical likelihood of π\pi is not too large with high probability, and hence π\pi cannot be a maximum-likelihood solution.

Let c∈(0,1/2)c\in(0,1/2) be the absolute constant in Section 4, and let C≥log⁡4C\geq{}\log{}4 be another absolute constant. Fix NN such that log⁡N≥4​C\log{}N\geq{}4C. For each model π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, let 𝒮N​(π):=1n​|{i∈[n]∣πD​(yi∣xi)π⁡(yi∣xi)≥N1−2​c}|\mathcal{S}_{N}(\pi)\vcentcolon={}\frac{1}{n}\lvert\big\{i\in[n]\mid{}\frac{\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}})}{\pi(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}})}\geq{}N^{1-2c}\big\}\rvert denote the empirical probability that π\pi fails to cover πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}. Our first step is to show via covering and concentration that with high-probability, all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi satisfy

𝒮N​(π)≥12​CovN​(π)−𝒞coarse​(Π,N,n).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{N}(\pi)\geq\frac{1}{2}\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi)-\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{coarse}}(\Pi,N,n). (10)

That is, a large coverage profile implies that the number of points in the data where π\pi fails to cover πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} is large. This argument only depends on the covering number at a coarse log⁡N\log{}N scale—leading to the coarse-grained term in Section 4---because we only need to show that coverage concentrates, not the log-loss itself.55 5 The set 𝒮N​(π)\mathcal{S}_{N}(\pi) is defined with the threshold as N1−2​cN^{1-2c} rather than NN to account for approximation errors incurred by covering.

We now argue that models with large coverage profile must have low log-likelihood compared to πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}. In particular, using Eq. 10, we have

Next, using a variation of a standard one-sided tail bound for the logarithmic loss (van de Geer, 2000; Zhang, 2006),66 6 That the bound is one-sided is critical, as this allows us to avoid paying for the range of the density ratios under consideration. For details, see Section H.1. we show that with high probability, all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi satisfy

∑i=1nlog⁡π⁡(yi∣xi)πD​(yi∣xi)∨(−C)≲𝒞fine​(Π,n)⋅n,\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\frac{\pi(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}})}{\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}})}\vee(-C)\lesssim{}\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{fine}}(\Pi,n)\cdot{}n, (12)

as long as C≥log⁡4C\geq\log 4. Combining Eq. 11 and Eq. 12, we conclude that all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi have

Since the maximum likelihood estimator π^\widehat{\pi} has L^n​(πD)−L^n​(π^)≤0\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi_{\texttt{D}})-\widehat{L}_{n}(\widehat{\pi})\leq{}0, the result follows.

To summarize the key ideas as they relate to the final guarantee in Section 4: The coarse-grained term 𝒞coarse​(Π,N,n)\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{coarse}}(\Pi,N,n) enters because we only need to show that the coverage profile concentrates, not the log loss itself. The fine-grained term 𝒞fine​(Π,n)\mathcal{C}_{\texttt{fine}}(\Pi,n) enters concentration of the empirical likelihood, with the 1/log⁡N1/\log{}N scaling arising from implicit bias. The reason this argument avoids dependence on the sequence length HH or other spurious parameters that would otherwise affect cross-entropy is that the argument is fundamentally one-sided: the conclusion Eq. 13 only shows that models with large coverage profile have low log-likelihood compared to πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}.

Discussion

We emphasize that while covering numbers are a fundamental and widely used notion of capacity in statistical learning and estimation (van de Geer, 2000; Zhang, 2002; Rakhlin and Sridharan, 2012; Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014; Bilodeau et al., 2023), they are conservative from a modern generalization perspective. Nonetheless, Section 4 shows that they are sufficient to capture rich aspects of generalization for coverage, and we expect that our core analysis techniques can be combined with contemporary advances in generalization theory for overparameterized models (Belkin et al., 2019; Bartlett et al., 2020).

We believe there are many exciting avenues for refined results that build on the basic techniques here. For example, in Section E.1 (Section E.1), we show that for convex model classes, the coverage profile for maximum likelihood converges at a 1/poly⁡(N)1/\mathrm{poly}(N) rate instead of the 1/log⁡N1/\log{}N rate in Section 4.

4.3 Tightness of Theorem 4

To conclude, we show that the coarse and fine-grained terms in Section 4 are both tight in general. {proposition} The following lower bounds on coverage hold for the maximum likelihood estimator.

(a) Coarse rate: For any n≥d≥2n\geq d\geq 2 and B≥log⁡(5​n)B\geq\log(5n), there exists a class Π\Pi with log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,α)≲d​log⁡(B/α)∨1\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha)\lesssim d\log(B/\alpha)\vee{}1 and πD∈Π\pi_{\texttt{D}}\in\Pi such that with probability at least 0.50.5, it holds that for any N≤eBN\leq e^{B},

CovN​(π^)≥c⋅dn.\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\geq c\cdot\frac{d}{n}.

(b) Fine rate: For any d≥1,n≥2​d,N≥2d\geq 1,n\geq 2d,N\geq 2, there exists a class Π\Pi and πD∈Π\pi_{\texttt{D}}\in\Pi such that |Π|=2d+1\lvert\Pi\rvert=2^{d}+1 and 𝒩∞​(Π,α)≤2\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\alpha)\leq 2 for any α≥dn\alpha\geq\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}, and with probability at least 0.10.1, it holds that

CovN​(π^)≥c⋅dn⋅log⁡N.\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\geq c\cdot\frac{d}{n\cdot\log N}.

Informally, case (a) shows that for the class Π\Pi under consideration, the coverage does not decrease with log⁡N\log{}N until NN is trivially large such that log⁡𝒩∞​(Π,log⁡N)=0\log\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\Pi,\log{}N)=0; this is precisely the behavior of the coarse term in Section 4, so this implies there is no hope of removing this term. Meanwhile, case (b) can be interpreted as showing that there is no hope of replacing the high-precision covering number found in the fine-grained term in Section 4 with a coarser notion (e.g, at the scale in the coarse-grained term), since the rate grows with d≈log⁡|Π|d\approx\log\lvert\Pi\rvert even though log⁡𝒩⁡(Π,α)\log\mathcal{N}(\Pi,\alpha) is constant for α≥dn\alpha\geq\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}. We note that Section 4.3 is an algorithm-specific lower bound, not an information-theoretic lower bound; we show in Section 6.3 that it is possible to improve over Section 4 with algorithms explicitly designed to optimize for coverage.

5 Stochastic Gradient Descent Through the Lens of Coverage

The coverage-based generalization guarantees for next-token prediction in the prequel apply to general model classes Π\Pi, but consider the empirical maximizer π^=arg​maxπ∈Π⁡L^n​(π)\widehat{\pi}=\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi}\widehat{L}_{n}(\pi) of the next-token prediction (maximum likelihood) objective, in the vein of classical techniques in learning theory. For our second set of main results, we focus on autoregressive linear models (3) but take a more realistic approach and analyze stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the next-token prediction objective, in the single-pass regime. This setup is motivated by contemporary (“compute-optimal”) language model training, which typically uses one or fewer passes over the training corpus (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022).

5.1 Stochastic Gradient Descent has Suboptimal Coverage

For the next-token prediction objective, single-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD) takes the form77 7 ProjΘ⁡(⋅)\Proj_{\Theta}(\cdot) denotes Euclidean projection onto Θ\Theta, so this is the SGD update on the loss L⁡(θ):=𝔼⁡[−log⁡πθ​(y∣x)]L(\theta)\vcentcolon=\En[-\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)].

θt+1←ProjΘ(θt+η∇logπθt(yt∣xt)),\displaystyle\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t+1}}\leftarrow\Proj_{\Theta}\left(\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}+\eta\nabla\log\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}}(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}\mid x^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}})\right), (14)

for xt∼μx^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}\sim\mu and yt∼πD(⋅∣xt)y^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}\sim\pi_{\texttt{D}}(\cdot\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}), where η>0\eta>0 is the learning rate. As the next-token prediction loss L⁡(θ):=𝔼πD⁡[−log⁡πθ​(y∣x)]L(\theta)\vcentcolon=\En_{\pi_{\texttt{D}}}[-\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)] is convex under the parameterization (3), we can show that SGD converges to πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} in KL divergence. This implies a coverage bound, albeit a suboptimal one.

{proposition}

[SGD for autoregressive linear models] Upper bound: Suppose Sections 2 and 2 hold. As long as η≤12​H​B2\eta\leq\frac{1}{2HB^{2}}, it holds that 𝔼[1T∑t=1TD𝖪𝖫(πD∥πθt)]≤4η​T+2ησ⋆2\En\big[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}}\right)\big]\leq\frac{4}{\eta{}T}+2\eta\sigma_{\star}^{2}. Choosing η\eta to minimize this bound gives

𝔼⁡[1T​∑t=1TCovN​(πθt)]≲1log⁡N⋅(σ⋆2T+B2​HT).\displaystyle\En\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}})\right]\lesssim\frac{1}{\log{}N}\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{T}}+\frac{B^{2}H}{T}\right). (15)

Lower bound: Suppose that B≥c⋅log2⁡(T​H)B\geq c\cdot\log^{2}(TH). Then there exists an autoregressive linear class Π\Pi such that for any constant step size η>0\eta>0, there exists an instance πD∈Π\pi_{\texttt{D}}\in\Pi with σ⋆≤1\sigma_{\star}\leq 1 such that with probability at least 0.50.5, the SGD iterates satisfy

CovN(πD∥πθt)≥c⋅min{HT​log⁡N,1},∀t∈[T].\displaystyle\texttt{Cov}_{N}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}}\right)\geq c\cdot\min\left\{\frac{H}{T\log N},1\right\},\qquad\forall t\in[T]. (16)

The coverage bound in Eq. 15 (which follows by passing from KL to coverage through Section 3) is similar to Section 4.1, except that the second term B2​HT\frac{B^{2}H}{T} has an unfortunate dependence on the sequence length HH. The lower bound in Eq. 16 shows that this dependence is tight, and SGD can indeed experience poor coverage. This failure of SGD is related to heterogeneity across prompts: there are some prompts for which the effective scale of the gradient in Eq. 14 grows with HH, leading to divergence unless we use a small learning rate η≲1H​B\eta\lesssim\frac{1}{HB}. Yet for other prompts, the effective gradient range is small, leading to slow convergence (on the order of Ω⁡(H)\Omega(H) steps) unless η≫1H​B\eta\gg\frac{1}{HB}.

{remark}

[Sequence-level SGD] The update in Eq. 14 can be interpreted as a “sequence-level” form of SGD, since we perform a single gradient step for each full sequence yty^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}} (note that ∇logπθt(yt∣xt)=∑h=1H∇logπθt(yht∣xt,y1:h−1t)\nabla\log\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}}(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}})=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\nabla\log\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}}(y_{h}^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}\mid{}x^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}},y_{1:h-1}^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}})). We view this as a model for what is done in practice, whereby one performs SGD on sequences of tokens spanning some fixed context window. While this context window may be shorter than the full training example (e.g., a long article), understanding the implications of a limited context window is beyond the scope of this work.

5.2 Gradient Normalization Improves Coverage

To address the suboptimality of SGD, we consider gradient normalization as a simple intervention. For a mini-batch 𝒟={(xi,yi)}i=1K\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}},y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}})\right\}_{i=1}^{K} of KK samples from πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}, define the batch stochastic gradient as

g^​(θ,𝒟)=1|𝒟|​∑(x,y)∈𝒟∇log⁡πθ​(y∣x).\displaystyle\widehat{g}(\theta;\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}}\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). (17)

We consider the following normalized SGD update:

θt+1←ProjΘ⁡(θt+η⋅g^​(θt,𝒟t)λ+‖g^​(θt,𝒟t)‖);\displaystyle\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t+1}}\leftarrow\Proj_{\Theta}\left(\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}+\eta\cdot\frac{\widehat{g}(\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}};\mathcal{D}^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}})}{\lambda+\|\widehat{g}(\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}};\mathcal{D}^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}})\|}\right); (18)

here 𝒟t\mathcal{D}^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}} is a mini-batch with KK fresh samples drawn i.i.d. from πD\pi_{\texttt{D}}, and λ>0\lambda>0 is a regularization parameter for numerical stability. We show that this update achieves a horizon-independent coverage bound.{theorem} Suppose Section 2 and Section 2 hold. Let T,K≥1,N≥3T,K\geq 1,N\geq 3 be given. For an appropriate choice of η,λ>0\eta,\lambda>0, the normalized SGD update (18) achieves the following coverage bound:

𝔼⁡[1T​∑t=1TCovN​(πθt)]≲σ⋆2T⋅log⁡N+B2T+BK⋅log⁡N.\displaystyle\En\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}})\right]\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{T\cdot\log N}}+\frac{B^{2}}{T}+\frac{B}{K\cdot\log N}. (19)

To achieve 𝔼⁡[CovN​(π^)]≤ε\En\left[\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\widehat{\pi})\right]\leq\varepsilon for a target level ε>0\varepsilon>0, it suffices to choose T=O⁡(σ⋆2ε2​log⁡N+B2ε)T=O\big(\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}\log N}+\frac{B^{2}}{\varepsilon}\big), K=O⁡(Bε​log⁡N+1)K=O\big(\frac{B}{\varepsilon\log N}+1\big), giving total sample complexity n=T​K=O⁡(σ⋆2​Bε3​log2​N+B3+σ⋆2ε2​log⁡N+B2ε)n=TK=O\big(\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}B}{\varepsilon^{3}\log^{2}N}+\frac{B^{3}+\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}\log{}N}+\frac{B^{2}}{\varepsilon}\big). Section 5.2 shows that gradient normalization achieves horizon-independent coverage with a qualitatively similar rate to the guarantee for next-token prediction in Section 4.1: To achieve coverage ε\varepsilon, both rates scale as poly⁡(σ⋆2log⁡N,B,ε−1)\mathrm{poly}\big(\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{\log{}N},B,\varepsilon^{-1}\big), though the dependence on ε\varepsilon for Section 5.2 is worse. We emphasize that minibatching alone is not enough to achieve this result; rather, minibatching is necessary to avoid excessive bias once we introduce gradient normalization.

Somewhat speculatively, we believe that it may be possible to use similar techniques to Section 5.2 to show that Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) and relatives enjoy improved coverage relative to SGD. Adam is believed to behave similarly to the SignSGD update (Balles and Hennig, 2018; Bernstein et al., 2018; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024), which takes the form

θt+1←θt+η⋅sign⁡(g^​(θt,𝒟t)).\displaystyle\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t+1}}\leftarrow\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}+\eta\cdot\mathrm{sign}\big(\widehat{g}(\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}};\mathcal{D}^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}})\big). (20)

In fact, Adam reduces to Eq. 20 when EMA and bias correction are disabled. This is very similar form of gradient normalization to Eq. 18, except that it normalizes per-coordinate rather than globally; this distinction is important for deep learning models, where different modules or layers can have very different scales, but we expect that it grants similar benefits with respect to sequence length.

6 Interventions for Better Coverage

In this section, we develop new interventions that improve coverage (and downstream performance) beyond the conventional algorithms analyzed in Sections 4 and 5. We view these results as promising proofs of concept for further research into interventions driven by coverage.

6.1 Improving Coverage at Test Time

In this section, we show that a new test-time decoding strategy inspired by test-time training (Sun et al., 2020; Akyürek et al., 2025) leads to improved coverage when combined with token-level SGD.

We focus on autoregressive linear models, but depart from Eq. 14 by learning models with a token-level SGD update, defined as

θt,h+1=ProjΘ(θt,h+η∇logπθt,h(yht∣xt,y1:h−1t)),for h=0,⋯,H−1,\displaystyle\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t,h+1}}=\Proj_{\Theta}\left(\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t,h}}+\eta\nabla\log\pi_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t,h}}}(y^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}_{h}\mid x^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}},y^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}_{1:h-1})\right),~~\text{for }h=0,\cdots,H-1, (21)

and θt+1≡θt+1,0:=θt,H\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t+1}}\equiv\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t+1,0}}\vcentcolon=\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t,H}} for t∈[T]t\in[T], and where (xt,y1:Ht)∼πD(x^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}},y^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}_{1:H})\sim\pi_{\texttt{D}}. We will show that—when combined with a test-time training-like update that performs token-level gradient updates during test time—the updates in Eq. 21 can circumvent the HH-dependence in the lower bound of Section 5.1.

Concretely, for a parameter θ\theta and prompt xx, define the following test-time parameter update recursively for h=0,1,⋯,H−1h=0,1,\cdots,H-1:

ϑTTT(x,y1:h;θ):=ProjΘ(ϑTTT(x,y1:h−1;θ)+η∇logπϑTTT(x,y1:h−1;θ)(yh∣x,y1:h−1)).\displaystyle\vartheta^{\texttt{TTT}}(x,y_{1:h};\theta)\vcentcolon=\Proj_{\Theta}\left(\vartheta^{\texttt{TTT}}(x,y_{1:h-1};\theta)+\eta\nabla\log\pi_{\vartheta^{\texttt{TTT}}(x,y_{1:h-1};\theta)}(y_{h}\mid x,y_{1:h-1})\right). (22)

We then define a distribution πθTTT:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴H)\pi^{\texttt{TTT}}_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}^{H}) as

πθTTT(⋅∣x,y1:h−1):=πϑTTT(x,y1:h−1;θ)(⋅∣x,y1:h−1).\displaystyle\pi^{\texttt{TTT}}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{1:h-1})\vcentcolon=\pi_{\vartheta^{\texttt{TTT}}(x,y_{1:h-1};\theta)}(\cdot\mid x,y_{1:h-1}). (23)

The distribution πθTTT\pi^{\texttt{TTT}}_{\theta} can be interpreted as an augmented version of the autoregressive linear model πθ\pi_{\theta} that performs test-time training during sampling: Given a prompt xx, we first sample y1∼πθ(⋅∣x)y_{1}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), then perform a gradient step θ′←ProjΘ(θ+η∇logπθ(y1∣x))\theta^{\prime}\leftarrow\Proj_{\Theta}\left(\theta+\eta\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{1}\mid x)\right) to increase the probability of the token we just sampled. We then sample y2∼πθ′(⋅∣x,y1)y_{2}\sim\pi_{\theta^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{1}), update θ′′←ProjΘ(θ′+η∇logπθ′(y2∣x,y1))\theta^{\prime\prime}\leftarrow\Proj_{\Theta}\left(\theta^{\prime}+\eta\nabla\log\pi_{\theta^{\prime}}(y_{2}\mid x,y_{1})\right), and so on. Once the full sequence y1:Hy_{1:H} is sampled, we reset back to θ\theta (so that we can process the next test-time example). We show that when augmented with this test-time sampling scheme, token-level SGD achieves a horizon-independent coverage bound that matches and even slightly improves upon the bound for next-token prediction in Section 4.1.{theorem}[Token-level SGD with test-time training] Suppose Section 2 and Section 2 hold. For a suitably chosen parameter η>0\eta>0, token-level SGD (21) achieves 𝔼[1T∑t=1TD𝖪𝖫(πD∥πθtTTT)]≲σ⋆2T+B2T\En\big[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi_{\texttt{D}}\,\|\,\pi^{\texttt{TTT}}_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}}\right)\big]\lesssim~\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{T}}+\frac{B^{2}}{T}, and thus

𝔼⁡[1T​∑t=1TCovN​(πθtTTT)]≲1log⁡N⋅(σ⋆2T+B2T).\displaystyle\En\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\texttt{Cov}_{N}(\pi^{\texttt{TTT}}_{\theta^{{\scriptscriptstyle t}}})\right]\lesssim\frac{1}{\log N}\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\star}^{2}}{T}}+\frac{B^{2}}{T}\right).

This improves Section 4.1 by a factor of 1/log⁡N1/\sqrt{\log N} on the leading term and a factor of 1/log⁡N1/\log{}N on the second term. Furthermore, the algorithm bypasses the lower bound on KL divergence for proper methods in Section 3, demonstrating a provable benefit of being improper.

6.2 SGD: Improved Gradient Normalization for Distillation

We next consider a variant of our setting inspired by distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016). We assume that for each example (xi,y1:Hi)(x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}},y^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}_{1:H}), for each h=1,…,Hh=1,\ldots,H, we have access to the true next-token probabilities πD(yh∣xi,y1:h−1i)\pi_{\texttt{D}}(y_{h}\mid x^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}},y_{1:h-1}^{{\scriptscriptstyle i}}) for all yh∈𝒱y_{h}\in\mathcal{V}. This is natural for distillation, where πD\pi_{\texttt{D}} corresponds to a teacher model (in particular, the next-token probabilities are already computed as part of a standard forward pass through the teacher model). For the distillation setting, we give an improved gradient normalization scheme that improves upon the rate achieved by Section 5.2, closing the gap between SGD and maximum likelihood by matching the guarantee for Section 4.1.

Define ϵθ(x,y1:h−1):=D𝖪𝖫(πD(⋅∣x,y1:h−1)∥πθ(⋅∣x,y1:h−1))\epsilon_{\theta}(x,y_{1:h-1})
